extracted.intended_audience: journalism researchers, newspaper editors, reporters, and journalism educators
extracted.subtask_description: A field-experiment rubric for producing and evaluating newspaper news stories using four distinct writing modes (Traditional, Narrative, Radical Clarity, Point of View) and multiple reader-centered outcome measures (Reading, Involvement, Quality, Knowledge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional (inverted-pyramid) mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on the inverted pyramid: reporter writes a compelling lead and arranges subsequent material in descending order of importance; tone stays neutral, with more telling than showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production advantage: story can be shortened by deleting from the bottom; suits production needs. Criticisms: conservatism and pace keep journalists from expanding repertoire, may bore and confuse readers, places background/context late so readers without that background cannot fully understand the top of the story, reporters often assume more knowledge than readers possess; tends to lose readers halfway down the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Tells a story, with actions performed by characters in time sequences, including some chronological telling; each story has a beginning, middle and end; actions and speeches reveal motives; quotations retain characteristics of actual speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes 'showing' with a little 'telling'; familiar expectations to a wide population and effective as extended discourse. In the experiment narrative kept readers reading and had strong effects on some groups' learning and involvement, but sometimes failed to get readers involved in issues (descriptive tradeoffs to consider).

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical Clarity mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Arranges material to maximize reader understanding and explains whatever the reader might need explained; background and context appear early; can use second person; defines terms often and explains motives explicitly; attempts to 'take the reader's point of view.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design intent: shape the story to readers' needs and interests to increase comprehension. Limitation: hampered by making one story fit all needs and risks becoming an outline or boring if used for entire stories; works well for conveying information and for portions/sidebars that explain key facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of View mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Tells the story with a viewpoint that is immediately clear; tone ventures just short of the normative line between straight news and editorializing; uses shapes other than inverted pyramid and has a forceful ending that leaves the reader with the writer's central point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to persuade by showing rather than telling; can use second person. Experimental finding: often rated low on quality by many readers though it sometimes increases involvement and learning for particular subgroups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading (how much of the story was read) — dependent variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of whether the reader read the first few paragraphs, more than the first few paragraphs, or most or all of the treatment story (interviews terminated for respondents who had read only the headline or lead sentence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalized in telephone and questionnaire instruments; scores standardized to range between -1 and +1 (group mean = 0). Used as an outcome to judge how well a writing mode captures and retains readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involvement — dependent variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor composed of four 1–10 items: 'How much did you care about what happened in the article?', 'How much did you connect the article to other issues or your own experiences?', 'How much did reading this article make you want to find out more about issues like this?', and 'How much did reading this article make you want to get more directly involved in issues like this?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from factor analysis; independent of Quality (readers can feel involved without rating a story high on quality). Used to evaluate the mode's ability to induce civic or personal engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality — dependent variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor composed of two 1–10 items: 'How would you rate how well the (treatment) article was written?' and 'On the same scale, how balanced and accurate was the writing for this article?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from factor analysis; treated as a reader perception of writing craft and fairness; in path analyses Quality sometimes mediates learning (e.g., Traditional required high-quality judgment before learning occurred).

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge — dependent variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite score from four true-or-false questions related to basic factual information contained in all four versions of a story; higher number of correct responses yields a higher standardized score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an objective measure of whether readers learned facts from the story; standardized between -1 and +1 in analyses. Path analysis examined routes from Reading/Involvement/Quality to Knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'substantial' effect / scoring convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Scores for dependent variables were standardized to range between -1 and +1 (group mean = 0). A 'substantial' difference was defined as a score deviating from its group mean by more than 5 percent of the possible variation for that dependent variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because some cells lacked power for traditional p < .05 tests, the authors treated >5% deviation as an indicator of an important, possibly significant effect (these deviations are denoted by asterisks in the tables).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental design validity controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Controls included: four reporters rotating through all four writing modes and circulation zones; each zone received all modes across days; identical photographs/graphics, identical headlines and identical subheads; identical story length and same jump position; reporters brainstormed jointly and shared background and quotes; researchers did not change content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rotation controls for reporter and zone effects; editorial constraints preserved normal journalistic standards while ensuring treatments differed by writing mode only. These design features are criteria for valid field experimentation in newsroom environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling and survey procedure standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Daily telephone survey by cluster sampling from subscriber lists (clusters = carrier routes) with equal-sized clusters within each zone; respondents were screened for having read the treatment story; additional convenience sample of vocational-technical college students given shuffled packets of four local sections and given 30 minutes to read and complete the same instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combination of cross-sectional subscriber surveys and targeted technical-college sampling was used to ensure representation of younger, less-educated, less-loyal readers; variation due to survey method was controlled as a covariate in Multiple Classification Analysis (MCA). Response rates around 50% each night; sample sizes ~217–250 per day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study hypotheses as evaluative expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Five main-effect hypotheses and one interaction hypothesis were specified: H1: Knowledge scores highest for Radical Clarity. H2: Involvement measures highest for Narrative and Point of View modes. H3: Quality measures highest for Traditional and lowest for Point of View. H4: Reading highest for Narrative, Traditional lowest. H5: In aggregate Traditional will score no better than any alternative mode. H6 (interaction): Younger, less-educated, less-frequent readers will produce higher scores with Narrative and Radical Clarity and lower scores with Traditional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses provide explicit expectations to judge modes against; results are reported relative to these a priori criteria and used to interpret which modes 'work better' for particular outcomes and subgroups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Path-analysis criterion: routes from Reading to Knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Path analyses examined influences among Reading, Story Quality, Story Involvement and Knowledge and found mode-specific routes: Traditional—readers needed to believe story was high quality to learn; Narrative—some learned directly by reading and some via quality; Radical Clarity—reading or involvement led to learning with quality judgments less relevant; Point of View—learning occurred only if readers believed the story to be high quality or became involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use path-structure as a diagnostic rubric: choose a mode according to intended route to learning (e.g., Narrative if direct path from reading to knowledge is desired; Radical Clarity for conveying information when narrative is inappropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial recommendation: combine modes and use complementary devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should consider creative combinations of styles (e.g., storytelling technique to capture interest plus a 'radically clear' sidebar to communicate hard information; include a hard summary box so narrative readers can find the 'nut graph').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical production guideline: no single style is superior for all goals; select mode(s) based on whether the story chiefly seeks to induce readership, convey substantial information, entertain, or move the reader to action. Encourage frequent use of storytelling components and selective use of radical clarity for portions of stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoided conventional practices that impede comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventional newswriting practices identified as potential deterrents to reading: inverted-pyramid overuse, block paragraphs, artificial transitions, choppy sentences and paragraphs, and organization optimized for production convenience rather than readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These characteristics are presented as anti-patterns; the rubric implies favoring techniques that reduce such features (e.g., provide context earlier, improve narrative coherence, define terms) to make stories more accessible to aliterate readers.
